οὐκοῦν [therefore] (syllogistic, as the grammarians call it) means therefore, without interrogation, although this very meaning arose from interrogation, as Hermann noted. For otherwise the negation οὐκ [not] could not be present.

On the difference in meaning between οὐκοῦν [therefore] and οὔκουν [not therefore] see Apollonius in Bekker's Anecdota p. 525-526 and Ammonius p. 105. Phrynichus in Bekker's Anecdota p. 57, 10: οὐκοῦν [therefore]: with the circumflex it has a syllogistic sense, but with the acute accent it is taken in two ways among the Attic writers, sometimes instead of μόλις [scarcely] used in negation, sometimes by transposition: οὔκουν ἐάσεις [will you not allow?] = οὐκ ἐάσεις οὖν [will you not then allow?]. And in Aristophanes (fr. 518) “οὔκουν μ᾽ ἐάσεις ἀναμετρήσασθαι τάδε;” [Will you not allow me to measure out these things?] instead of οὐκ ἐάσεις οὖν με [will you not then allow me?]. On both Hermann has spoken in his notes on Viger p. 794-795 and L. Dindorf in the Thesaurus vol. 5 p. 2378. The copyists paid little attention to the distinction in meaning which the grammarians establish, and often wrote οὐκοῦν [therefore] where οὔκουν [not therefore] should have been written.
